newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Quarter of Hungarian computer sales said illegal.
newsitem.headline: Quarter of Hungarian computer sales said illegal.

text.p: Up to 25 percent of Hungary's total sales of computers are illegal, industry sources said on Monday.

"We think the (computer) hardware black market accounts for up to a quarter of Hungary's information technology turnover," Tibor Gyuros, president of the Information Enterprises Association (IVSZ) told Reuters.
Gyuros, who is also the general director of computer firm Rolitron Rt, said the IVSZ met with tax and customs officials at the weekend to tackle the growing black market. @
Another industry source said information technology annual turnover is estimated to be some 100 billion forints a year, with personal computers (PC) and printers making up 60 to 65 percent.
"Roughly one-third of PCs and printers arrive illegally in the country," said Gyorgy Beck, general director of Digital Hungary, a unit of U.S.-based Digital Equipment Corp.
He estimated that as much as 90 percent of computer memory chips could come from illegal imports, but hard disks, motherboards and processors also feature heavily on the list. @
One unregistered Hungarian company sold last year 4.6 billion forints ($30 million) worth of bootleg computers, Beck revealed.
However, other firms are more seriously hit by the thriving black market than Digital, the core business of which is the supply of corporate buyers.
Although unable to give figures, the world's largest processor manufacturer, Intel 's Hungarian representative said the problem is real. @
"Processor black market is probably on the same scale as hard disk black market," said Peter Kovacs of Intel Hungary Ltd.
The high proportion of illegal products also means a larger price gap between brand-name and no-name computers, Beck said.

"Hungary has a two-to-one ratio in prices, while in western countries this ratio is somewhere around 1.4," he said, adding that the unreliability and poor servicing of illegally sold products has a negative effect on the whole industry. @
"People who buy cheap and often unreliable computers will end up with a bad opinion about computers in general," Beck said.
